'''''Uragasaurus''''' ({{lit|serpent lizard}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[mamenchisaurid]] sauropod dinosaur known from the [[Late Jurassic]] [[Phu Kradung Formation]] of Thailand. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Uragasaurus kalasinensis''''', known from a single dorsal (trunk) vertebra. It is the first member of the family Mamenchisauridae named from Thailand.

== Discovery and naming ==
{{multiple image
 | align = left

The ''Uragasaurus'' fossil material was discovered in outcrops of the lower [[Phu Kradung Formation]] (Phu Noi locality), part of the [[Khorat Group]], in [[Kalasin Province]] of northeastern Thailand. The specimen is housed in the Palaeontological Research and Education Centre (PRC) at [[Mahasarakham University]], where it is permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen PRC 460. It consists of a single [[Anatomical terms of location#Anterior and posterior|anterior]] (toward the front) {{dinogloss|dorsal vertebra}}. [[Taphonomic]] compression has flattened the bone anteroposteriorly (from front to back).<ref name="Uragasaurus" />

In 2026, Apirut Nilpanapan and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Uragasaurus kalasinensis'' as a new genus and species of mamenchisaurid sauropod based on these fossil remains, establishing PRC 460 as the [[holotype]] specimen. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Uragasaurus'', combines the [[Sanskrit]] word उरग, meaning {{gloss|serpent}} or {{gloss|snake}}, with the [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|[[wikt:σαῦρος#Etymology|σαῦρος]]}} ({{lang|grc|saûros}}), meaning {{gloss|lizard}}. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''kalasinensis'', references the discovery of the species in Kalasin Province.<ref name="Uragasaurus" />

A middle {{dinogloss|cervical vertebra}}, right {{dinogloss|cervical rib}}, two anterior dorsal vertebral {{dinogloss|neural arches}} and a mid-[[Anatomical terms of location#Anterior and posterior|posterior]] (toward the rear) dorsal vertebra, a left {{dinogloss|coracoid}}, and a left {{dinogloss|fibula}} were found disarticulated but in close association with the holotype of ''U. kalasinensis''. They cannot be confidently referred to this species due to the absence of shared or diagnostic anatomical features.<ref name="Uragasaurus" />

An isolated dorsal vertebra from the mid-late Jurassic [[Khlong Min Formation]] of Thailand was described by [[Éric Buffetaut|Buffetaut]] et al. in 2005, which represents the oldest mamenchisaurid occurrence in Southeast Asia.<ref name="Buffetaut2005" /> Suteethorn et al. (2013) then described a posterior {{dinogloss|cervical vertebra}} from the Phu Kradung Formation (Phu Dan Ma locality).<ref name="Suteethorn2012" /> These specimens remained unnamed, making ''Uragasaurus'' the first mamenchisaurid from the country to be given a scientific name.<ref name="Uragasaurus" />

== Description ==
[[File:Uragasaurus kalasinensis (life restoration).png|thumb|[[Paleoart|Paleoenvironmental reconstruction]] of five ''U. kalasinensis'' individuals]]
Nilpanapan et al. (2026) recognized a single [[autapomorphy]] (unique derived character) distinguishing ''Uragasaurus'' from all other mamenchisaurids: the [[Anatomical terms of location#Proximal and distal|distal]] (toward the tip) end of the {{dinogloss|transverse processes}} on the anterior dorsal vertebra have a prominent {{dinogloss|fossa|pneumatic fossa}} in an elongate teardrop shape. More complete relatives are characterized by their greatly elongated necks.<ref name="Uragasaurus" />

== Classification ==
To test the affinities and relationships of ''Uragasaurus'', Nilpanapan et al. (2026) included it in an updated version of the [[phylogenetic]] matrix of Moore et al. (2023).<ref name="Moore2023" /> ''Uragasaurus'' was recovered as an early-diverging member of the [[eusauropod]] clade [[Mamenchisauridae]], diverging after ''[[Tienshanosaurus]]'' but before ''[[Qijianglong]]''. These results are displayed in the [[cladogram]] below. The relationships among mamenchisaurids in their analysis were weakly supported, partly due to the fragmentary nature of some taxa, such as ''Uragasaurus''. The clade including ''Tienshanosaurus'' and all more [[Basal (phylogenetics)|derived]] mamenchisaurids is supported by three anatomical characters, only one of which can be recognized in ''Uragasaurus'': the presence of a bifurcated (split into two) {{dinogloss|neural spine}} on the anterior dorsal vertebra.<ref name="Uragasaurus" />
